His saying, may He be exalted: "Leave Me with those who deny" is a threat to them. It is related that there was only a short interval between the revelation of this verse and Badr, about a year; but the matter is not so. The estimate supported by the evidence from the reports of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ requires that the interval between the two events was about ten years; but that is little. Grant them respite.

"Food that chokes" is the tree of zaqqum; this is said by Mujahid and others. It is also said: a thorn of fire that lodges in their throats, neither coming out nor going down; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Every food there is food that chokes. It is related that "the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and fainted."

"Al-rajafan" is trembling and agitation from fear and terror. "Al-mahil" is the soft, loose sand that is carried away and returned by the wind; thus it is "tahilah," and the original form is "mahyul." The damma was felt heavy on the ya', so it became quiescent; two quiescent letters met, so the waw was deleted, and the ha' was given a kasra because of the ya'.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿a witness over you﴾ is like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We bring you as a witness over these﴾ [an-Nisa: 41]. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾ means Musa, peace be upon him; the alif and lam are for prior reference. "Al-wabil" is the severe, bad in outcome; it is said: "kala' wabil wa mustawbil" when it is harmful to what grazes on it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then how will you guard yourselves﴾ means: how will you make a protection for yourselves? "Yawman" is the object of "tattaqun." It is also said that it is the object of "kafartum," taking it as equivalent to "jahadtum"; then "tattaqun," in this case, is from taqwa, meaning you guard against the punishment of Allah. It is permissible that "yawman" be an adverbial noun of time, and the meaning is: you guard against the punishment of Allah on a day. "Yaj'alu" may be attributed to the name of Allah, the Exalted, and it may be attributed to the Day. His saying, may He be exalted: "al-wildan" refers to young children. Others among the interpreters said: it is a figurative expression and an emphatic description of the terror of that day. The singular of "al-wildan" is "walid," and the singular of "al-shayb" is "ashyab."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 73, verses 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and [so do] a group of those with you. And Allah determines the night and the day. He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it, so He has turned to you in forgiveness. So recite what is easy of the Qur'an. He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others who fight in the way of Allah. So recite what is easy of it, and establish the prayer, and give zakah, and lend to Allah a goodly loan. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward. And seek forgiveness from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The reference of "this" (hadhihi) may be to what was mentioned of the shackles, the Hellfire, the severe punishment and the like; it may be to the whole surah; and it may be to the Qur'an, in the sense that the statements set forth in it are a reminder. The word "reminder" (tadhkirah) is a verbal noun like "remembrance" (dhikr). His saying, Exalted is He, "so whoever wills," does not mean permission to do a matter and its opposite; rather it includes the meaning of threat and promise. "The way" (al-sabil) here is the way of goodness and obedience.

His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed, your Lord knows," the verse was revealed as a lightening of what had long been practised regarding the standing in prayer at night, whether it was obligatory or recommended, according to the disagreement we have mentioned. The meaning of the verse is: Allah knows that you, and others of your community besides you, stand in prayer in varying degrees: sometimes more, sometimes less, sometimes nearer to two-thirds, and sometimes nearer to one-third. This is because humans cannot precisely reckon the measures of time, along with the difficulty of sleep. The determination of time in reality belongs to Allah Exalted; as for humans, they cannot count it. So Allah turned to them in forgiveness, that is, He brought them back from heaviness to lightness, and commanded them to recite what is easy of it.

This is what the expression of al-Farra' and Mundhir gives, for both said: "tuhsuhu" means "tahfazuhu" (you guard it). This interpretation is in accordance with the reading of those who read "wa-nisfihi wa-thuluthi" in the genitive, as a conjunction with "al-thuluthayn." This is the reading of Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir. As for those who read "wa-nisfahu wa-thuluthahu" in the accusative, as a conjunction with "adna," which is the reading of the rest of the Seven, the meaning for them is different. That is because Allah Exalted has decreed that they would measure the time in the manner He commanded in His saying, Exalted is He: "Half of it, or reduce from it a little" [al-Muzzammil: 3] "or add to it" [al-Muzzammil: 4]. So there remains only that the saying of Allah Exalted, "You will not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you," means: "You will not be able to sustain its standing because of its length and difficulty," so Allah lightened it for them out of His grace, not for the reason of their ignorance of the measurement and the counting of the times. The expression of al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr gives something similar to this, for both said: "tuhsuhu" means "tuti'uhu" (you obey it). The majority of reciters and people read "wa-thuluthuhu" with a damma on the lam, while Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl from him, read "wa-thuluthuhu" with a sukun on the lam.

His saying, Exalted is He, "So recite what is easy of the Qur'an" is a permission. This is the saying of the majority. Ibn Jubayr and a group said: it is an obligation that cannot be dispensed with, even if it is fifty verses. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin said: the standing in prayer at night is obligatory, even if it is the time needed to milk a sheep. However, al-Hasan said: whoever recites one hundred verses, the Qur'an will not argue against him. A group of scholars approved of this. Some of them said: the two rak'ahs after 'Isha' together with the witr enter under the ruling of this command and its fulfilment, and whoever adds, Allah Exalted will increase his reward.

The "inna" in His saying, Exalted is He, "He knows that" is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), and the implied sense is that "he will be," so the sin (sa) came as a replacement for the omitted element. Likewise "la" came in the verse of Abu Mihjan:

Do not bury me in the wilderness, for indeed I
fear, if I die, that I will not taste it.

"Darb fi al-ard" (travelling through the land) is travel for trade, while "darb al-ard" is walking for relieving oneself and for the open-air toilet. So Allah Exalted mentioned the excuses of the children of Adam which prevent them from standing in prayer at night, namely illness and travel for trade or for raiding, so He lightened the standing for them because of this. In this verse is the excellence of travelling through the land for trade and seeking provision, together with travel for jihad. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The death most beloved to me after being killed in the way of Allah is that I die between the two sides of my saddle, travelling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty."

Then Allah Exalted repeated the command to recite what is easy of it, for emphasis. The prayer and the zakah here are the obligatory ones. Whoever says that standing at night is not obligatory says: the meaning of the verse is: take from this voluntary act what is easy for you, and guard your obligatory duties. Whoever says that some of the standing is obligatory says: Allah joined it with the obligatory duties because it is an obligation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 73, verses 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and [so do] a group of those with you. And Allah determines the night and the day. He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it, so He has turned to you in forgiveness. So recite what is easy of the Qur'an. He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others who fight in the way of Allah. So recite what is easy of it, and establish the prayer, and give zakah, and lend to Allah a goodly loan. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward. And seek forgiveness from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The reference of "this" (hadhihi) may be to what was mentioned of the shackles, the Hellfire, the severe punishment and the like; it may be to the whole surah; and it may be to the Qur'an, in the sense that the statements set forth in it are a reminder. The word "reminder" (tadhkirah) is a verbal noun like "remembrance" (dhikr). His saying, Exalted is He, "so whoever wills," does not mean permission to do a matter and its opposite; rather it includes the meaning of threat and promise. "The way" (al-sabil) here is the way of goodness and obedience.

His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed, your Lord knows," the verse was revealed as a lightening of what had long been practised regarding the standing in prayer at night, whether it was obligatory or recommended, according to the disagreement we have mentioned. The meaning of the verse is: Allah knows that you, and others of your community besides you, stand in prayer in varying degrees: sometimes more, sometimes less, sometimes nearer to two-thirds, and sometimes nearer to one-third. This is because humans cannot precisely reckon the measures of time, along with the difficulty of sleep. The determination of time in reality belongs to Allah Exalted; as for humans, they cannot count it. So Allah turned to them in forgiveness, that is, He brought them back from heaviness to lightness, and commanded them to recite what is easy of it.

This is what the expression of al-Farra' and Mundhir gives, for both said: "tuhsuhu" means "tahfazuhu" (you guard it). This interpretation is in accordance with the reading of those who read "wa-nisfihi wa-thuluthi" in the genitive, as a conjunction with "al-thuluthayn." This is the reading of Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir. As for those who read "wa-nisfahu wa-thuluthahu" in the accusative, as a conjunction with "adna," which is the reading of the rest of the Seven, the meaning for them is different. That is because Allah Exalted has decreed that they would measure the time in the manner He commanded in His saying, Exalted is He: "Half of it, or reduce from it a little" [al-Muzzammil: 3] "or add to it" [al-Muzzammil: 4]. So there remains only that the saying of Allah Exalted, "You will not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you," means: "You will not be able to sustain its standing because of its length and difficulty," so Allah lightened it for them out of His grace, not for the reason of their ignorance of the measurement and the counting of the times. The expression of al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr gives something similar to this, for both said: "tuhsuhu" means "tuti'uhu" (you obey it). The majority of reciters and people read "wa-thuluthuhu" with a damma on the lam, while Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl from him, read "wa-thuluthuhu" with a sukun on the lam.

His saying, Exalted is He, "So recite what is easy of the Qur'an" is a permission. This is the saying of the majority. Ibn Jubayr and a group said: it is an obligation that cannot be dispensed with, even if it is fifty verses. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin said: the standing in prayer at night is obligatory, even if it is the time needed to milk a sheep. However, al-Hasan said: whoever recites one hundred verses, the Qur'an will not argue against him. A group of scholars approved of this. Some of them said: the two rak'ahs after 'Isha' together with the witr enter under the ruling of this command and its fulfilment, and whoever adds, Allah Exalted will increase his reward.

The "inna" in His saying, Exalted is He, "He knows that" is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), and the implied sense is that "he will be," so the sin (sa) came as a replacement for the omitted element. Likewise "la" came in the verse of Abu Mihjan:

Do not bury me in the wilderness, for indeed I
fear, if I die, that I will not taste it.

"Darb fi al-ard" (travelling through the land) is travel for trade, while "darb al-ard" is walking for relieving oneself and for the open-air toilet. So Allah Exalted mentioned the excuses of the children of Adam which prevent them from standing in prayer at night, namely illness and travel for trade or for raiding, so He lightened the standing for them because of this. In this verse is the excellence of travelling through the land for trade and seeking provision, together with travel for jihad. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The death most beloved to me after being killed in the way of Allah is that I die between the two sides of my saddle, travelling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty."
